After surviving in lane since the earliest days of Dota All-Stars, I can personally attest to the extreme struggle and hardship of learning the intricacies of this game down to the most grueling and insignificant details. If, despite the admonitions of other reviews or the warnings of your family and friends, you have still elected to proceed with this commitment to defend the Ancient, I implore you to weigh this short, solemn adjuration in advance. I believe the real truth is that concealed beneath the facade of entertainment, graphics, and gameplay lies the unperceived—and often perilous—illumination of critical life lessons. During your pursuits, you will experience equally unavoidable resistance from adversaries and allies alike in the form of unbridled mental suffering, childish derision, and violent ridicule. This will occur despite your most sincere attempts to maintain amicable collaboration. You will be required by others to delve deep within your heart and soul to personally bear accountability for even the slightest perceived flaws or indiscretions. There will be no amelioration from this vitriolic, sacrificial behavior of the masses; you must aspire to defy one and all in order to advance your knowledge and skill set. Once you embark on this journey, there will be moments of despair and resignation in which your mind will begin to abandon all hope—where personal improvement appears inconceivable. In these moments, you must battle yourself to find the strength to withstand the constant pressure of adversity and mend the fractures of intellectual stultification to discover your path to growth. For those who persist and remain stoic, these transient and recurring feelings of dejection and pessimism are succeeded by some of the greatest thrills and emotions one can experience. As with almost everything in life, your experience throughout your matches within Dota will be a reflection of the resolve you've established as you lift the threshold of your skill level through dedication, time, and mental investment. The accomplishments chiseled out of hard work among your loyal and trusted companions will form an eternal bond which will always be remembered. If you succeed in mastering the art of leading the Dire or Radiant to victory in this game, I truly believe there are no tasks in life too difficult for you to achieve.

I thought *Dota 2* was just another popular MOBA that everyone played because it was competitive. I was wrong. At first, it looks complicated. There are dozens of heroes, hundreds of abilities, items everywhere, and enough terminology to make you wonder if you accidentally enrolled in a university course. But somewhere along the way, you start understanding it. And then you're in trouble. The gameplay is incredibly deep. Every match can turn into a completely different experience depending on the heroes, players, builds, decisions, and the thousand tiny mistakes everyone makes along the way. The first few games can feel overwhelming. Then you learn one thing. Then another. Eventually, you realize you've spent hundreds of hours learning a game that still has more to teach you. The best part is how much your decisions matter. One good team fight can change everything. One terrible decision can throw an entire match. Sometimes you make the perfect play and feel like a genius. Sometimes you walk into the enemy team and immediately question every decision you've ever made. I've played games with simpler mechanics, easier learning curves, and much less stress. I don't remember most of them. I'll remember *Dota 2*. Some games are competitive because they want you to win. *Dota 2* is competitive because it wants you to become obsessed with figuring out why you lost. And then queue again. 100% recommended.

Dota 2 is a 5v5 moba strategy game that I have been playing for~ Oh... Oh, no... Flows [*]Dota 2 rewards reflexes... But it rewards strategic thinking much more. And the skill ceiling of strategic thinking in a game with so many variables is (team compositions, item combinations, map positioning, etc.) nearly endless. [*]The whole game is focused on mechanics. Going faster by following the flow of the rivers, having no vision of higher ground areas, most of the terrain obstacles being trees that you can destroy with extremely basic items or hills that you can pass over with abilities or items, there is a day and night cycle with the later giving you increased movement speed but reduced visibility... Dota 2's map is far more than a flat board that might as well be background, it's a core part of the game. [*]Speaking of, the map is BIG, especially compared to other mobas. Traversing it takes time, and this is very much intentional. Map awareness is one of the most important skills a player should have. And I suck at it. [*]Over 100 heroes to choose, each doing something extremely unique. You will get no copy-pasted characters here, despite the huge roster (and unlike "some other popular mobas"). There is a hero that becomes deadly in the night but is weak during the day, one that focuses on brainwashing jungle creeps to fight for him, another that becomes stronger in water terrains, another that destroys trees as part of his core mechanics and on and on. The gameplay variety is fantastic. [*]In fact the mechanics of each hero are so unique, that the interactions between their various moves and the items they can buy are completely chaotic and infinitely entertaining. In general I love the sandbox approach Dota takes with its individual hero/team builds. There is a series called "Dota WTF" on YouTube that releases weekly, showing compilations of absurd in-game interactions recorded by players, hilarious more often than not. At the time this review is written it is at episode 646... [*]Every hero is strong in his own right, but certain heroes are simply above the rest in terms of power/flexibility. The "reason" they are above the rest is the same mechanical complexity that makes them challenging to control in the first place. Invoker is the most obvious example (a character with 9 different ultis, formed through your QWE basic ability combinations), but he is far from the only one. [*]Heroes are strong in what they do, but hardly anyone has an all-purposes complete kit. Each hero has built-in weaknesses to their arsenal (e.g. no defensive options/slow movement speed/heavy mana reliance, etc. etc.), and a smart opponent will exploit them. You will need to take yours into account and either supplement them through item builds, or choose specific team combinations. It is not unusual for games to be decided before they even start, by which team has the better synergy. [*]Visually, each hero is unique (audibly as well actually, the voice acting is fantastic). This obviously includes a plethora of babes, the hottest of which being Templar Assassin, an Arab-dancer-themed babe with Psylocke's abilities (you are of course allowed to prefer another female character as your favorite. It's just that you're wrong.) The more monsterous designs are the highlight though (and they have the best cosmetics). [*]The cosmetics are not single skins, but parts of skins, that you can combine as you like. You will either be playing Barbie, activating Polymerization, or enacting your inner doctor Frankenstein. Other cosmetics called "personas" and "arcanas" even completely redesign the characters from the base model. On that note, a lot of the cosmetics are designed by players, viewable in the game's Steam workshop at any time, and you can actually vote which ones you like. [*]Budget-wise, cosmetics are really affordable, with lootbox releases being infrequent. [*]Cosmetics include UI elements. Map skins, announcer packs, custom UIs and many more. A player who uses one of these can freely share it with the rest of his team, applied in the same session instantly. [*]The dark fantasy aesthetics really do it for me. Dota doesn't aim for realistic OR cartoony graphics, in the style LoL does, but rather for intentionally edgy 3D visuals. And it works. [*]Players can program crazy variants of the standard Dota build, including new maps, characters or even gamestyles, and then share them through the "Arcade" tab of the game. Currently I am watching a single-player roguelike called "Emberfall", while a football-themed variant was trending last week. The engine freedom Valve provides with Dota (and all its games in general) is absurd. [*]The developers really go balls to the wall with the major patches. Absolutely no rule is set in stone, and every game aspect is liable to be experimented on. I wouldn't call it so much "evolving" as "mutating", but it's still very entertaining and great at maintaining your interest. Flaws [*]I am really not a fan of the direction Dota's storytelling has taken. The Marvel-style humor & Rick and Morty style of self-awareness is a very ill fit for Dota's dark fantasy aesthetics and cosmically horrifying original lore. [*]Frankly the map could use a lot more interactions. I was a huge fan of Heroes of the Storm and its fantastic map-objective approach, and I wish Dota would take more ques for it. [*]While there are some mildly fanservice-y outfits for the girls, Valve is intentionally being conservative with them, and that's a shame. [*]The lack of a proper hero ban system is really hurting the game. Some heroes are banned randomly at the start of every match, but, objectively this should have been the players' choice instead of an RNG result. [*]In general, RNG is far more prevalent in Dota than it should have been. Ranged attacks to someone on higher ground have a 25% miss chance, or so the game says, because it's quite common to miss 5+ shots in a row. An Ogre Magi might trigger his QWE kit once each... Or each of them might trigger 4 times in the span of 2 seconds. Items often have a chance to trigger their attack modifiers, rather than having them guaranteed. I get that "some" RNG is supposed to be a part of it, but hitting someone 10+ hits with a Spirit Breaker and not triggering a single bash can lead to some very understandable screen punches. [*]Items are generally separated into early game items, mid game items and late game items. The vast majority of early and mid game permanent items are used as materials for some late game item, essentially evolving into them. Unfortunately that is not the case for some of them, including 2 out of the 4 evolutions of your boots, an aura buffing item called "Vladimir's Offering" and many others. Therefore the optimal play is to simply sell those items in the late game and buy something entirely new. The problem is you liked those items, and would very much prefer to have an evolved version of them instead of just erasing them from your arsenal. [*]The isometric view makes navigating trees really difficult. Oftentimes it looks like there is a path for you, but there isn't, resulting in your character taking a route he really shouldn't have taken. When you are being chased, that usually results in your death. [*]Completely random disconnections are not too uncommon, along with a variety of other technical issues, such as the client having trouble synching with the coordinator. [*]At some point, you will run out of Ukraine death jokes for all the Russians infesting European servers, despite having a dedicated server of their own. Communications issues arise, since they never speak English. Thumps up, go play it and get humbled. Dota 2 is a fantastic moba, with heavy emphasis on strategy, fantastic audiovisual design, customization options and RNG elements that encourage you to learn new slurs.

After thousands of hours in Dota 2, I think I’ve finally discovered the best advice I can give to any new player: Don’t play Dota 2. Seriously. Go play League of Legends, ROV, Mobile Legends, or literally any other MOBA where the developers still appear to remember that their game has players. Valve’s approach to smurfing is honestly impressive — not because they’ve solved it, but because somehow, after all these years, smurf accounts are still being created, boosted, sold, and thrown into lower-ranked matches like they’re part of the official matchmaking experience. Maybe smurfing isn’t a problem anymore. Maybe it’s a feature. And if you think reaching a higher rank will finally improve your experience, congratulations — Valve has apparently been working hard to make that worse too. Just look at what has happened at the very top of the ladder. When even Rank 1 players can watch their rank collapse in ways that make the entire system look ridiculous, you really have to admire Valve’s dedication to making sure nobody feels safe — not beginners, not veterans, not even the best players in the game. Equal opportunity suffering. Beautiful. Then we have the “events.” Remember when a Dota event actually felt like an event? Now it feels more like Valve remembered Dota exists during their lunch break and said: “Uh… give them some cosmetics or something.” The International used to feel like the World Cup of esports. The prize pool was legendary, Battle Pass season was exciting, everyone talked about TI, and even people who weren’t playing regularly came back to the game. Now? What’s the prize pool going to be? Who knows. Are the rewards exciting? Not really. Does Valve seem excited about TI anymore? Apparently not. But hey, at least we can all be excited about whatever other project Valve is currently more interested in. At this point, Dota 2 doesn’t feel like a game Valve is actively trying to grow. It feels like an old pet they occasionally remember to feed. The funniest part is that Dota 2 is still an incredible game underneath all of this. The gameplay, complexity, strategy, heroes, and competitive depth are things very few games can match. And somehow, Valve’s greatest achievement is making people who love Dota recommend that other people never start playing it. That takes talent. So from someone who has wasted — sorry, invested — thousands of hours into Dota 2: Do yourself a favor. Play another MOBA. Play League. Play ROV. Play something where you can at least pretend the developers want new players to stay. Because judging by the smurf situation, matchmaking decisions, underwhelming events, shrinking excitement around The International, and Valve’s overall enthusiasm toward Dota… I’m starting to think Valve isn’t trying to save Dota 2 anymore. They’re just waiting to see how long it takes to die on its own. And knowing Valve, when that finally happens, we’ll probably get a blog post six months later saying: “Thanks for playing.”

Once you're muted, you can't even communicate objectives properly anymore. No shot calling. No warning teammates. No coordinating Roshan, smoke, or pushes. Congratulations—you've punished the player who's actually trying to win. Valve seriously needs to stop relying on this lazy auto-report garbage. Do some actual analysis before punishing people. Look at the replay. Look at the chat logs. Look at player behavior. Look at who was griefing and who was actually playing the damn game. Instead, the system is basically: "Got reported enough? Cool, here's your punishment." What a joke. The funniest part is that toxic party stacks have figured this system out and abuse the hell out of it. They know they can mass-report the solo player and the system just eats it up. This isn't improving the community. It's rewarding toxic behavior. The gameplay is still incredible, but the report and communication system has become absolute trash. It's one of the worst moderation systems I've seen in any competitive game. Fix the damn report system. Stop punishing players who are actually trying to win, and start punishing the people who are abusing the system. Wasn't really into MOBA's before this game. As far as MOBA's go, this game is best of the best. Every win feels very rewarding, and each loss has something to learn from it. There is so much depth in each part of the game, and it's very rare for any game, let alone a MOBA with 127 heroes to feel balanced. Between patches there are def some heroes that are stronger than others, but for 90% of the player base it doesn't really matter. Game knowledge and skill is way more important than what heroes you play that are strong at the moment. Every dota player has experienced being completely destroyed by some low tier hero that was played to the absolute maximum. The game isn't restrictive like other MOBA's. You can truly make some wild and wacky stuff work as long as you execute great. It is very rare for the correct play to be building the exact same items every game on a hero. Each game is dynamic, and you have to respond to what heroes and items the enemies have, trying to do the same thing every time just wont work. Overall, this is probably one of the best balanced, high skill ceiling MOBA's there is.

(Recommended, with the same enthusiasm one recommends a particularly involved religion) There is a moment, roughly four hundred hours into your relationship with Dota 2, when you look up from the screen, notice that it is dark outside, that several meals have gone unmentioned to your body, and that you have just spent eleven minutes arguing with four strangers about whether someone called "xXx_PudgeGod_xXx" should have bought a Black King Bar. It is at this moment that you understand, with the calm clarity of a man who has seen the Total Perspective Vortex and lived, that Dota 2 is not so much a video game as it is a weather system that has learned to hold a grudge.1 It begins innocently enough. Somewhere, a small green shop sells you boots. This seems reasonable. Boots are a known quantity; humanity has understood boots for some time. But then you are asked to choose from over a hundred heroes, each possessing between four and infinity abilities, several of which do not do what their names suggest and at least one of which summons a second, smaller version of yourself to die on your behalf, which, if you think about it for too long, and you will have time, because games run to the fifty-minute mark as a matter of house pride, raises troubling questions about identity that Douglas Adams would have handled with a towel and Terry Pratchett would have handled by introducing a footnote longer than the original sentence.2 The game does not want you to win. This should be stated plainly, because the tutorial is too polite to say it. The game wants you to almost win, forever, in ever-more-elaborate ways, the way the universe wants a soufflé to almost rise. You will lose games you dominated. You will win games you spent apologising for. Somewhere a small number called MMR will go up or down by an amount so precisely calibrated to feel meaningless that you will nonetheless stare at it the way sailors once stared at the horizon, looking for weather. And yet. And yet there is a particular, specific joym, not happiness, exactly, happiness is too small and well-behaved a word, that arrives when five people who have never met, who do not speak the same language, who are frankly a little worried about each other's life choices, click four buttons in the correct order and a fight that was unwinnable becomes, briefly, gloriously winnable. For about six seconds, Dota 2 makes perfect sense, the way the universe is said to make perfect sense to people right before they get flattened by an unlikely bus. Then someone facechecks a bush and it is over, and you queue again, because you are only human, and humans are the sort of species that, having been burned by fire, invent a game about being burned by fire, and play it every night for a decade. Recommended. Bring snacks. Bring patience. Do not bring your self-esteem; it will not survive contact with the enemy midlaner, and you will not miss it nearly as much as you'd expect. 1. A weather system, it should be noted, run by a small Icelandic company that occasionally releases seventy pages of patch notes at three in the morning, changing the fundamental nature of reality for reasons that make sense to exactly one (1) person, who does not work there any more. ↩ 2. The footnote in question would eventually explain that yes, technically, the clone can also die to Roshan, and no, this does not entitle you to a refund on your sense of self. ↩

I installed Dota 2 expecting a competitive multiplayer game. What I received was an unpaid apprenticeship in human suffering. There are games where you learn mechanics, improve your reflexes, develop strategies, and eventually become better than you were before. Dota takes a more ambitious approach. It attempts to reconstruct your entire personality from the ground up. You begin with confidence. You select a hero. You buy your starting items. You walk towards the lane with the quiet optimism of someone who has absolutely no idea what is about to happen. Ten minutes later, your Russian teammate is furiously typing because you didn't rotate. You don't know what he is saying, but you understand the emotional meaning. Apparently you have committed an international crime. This is one of Dota's greatest features: the extraordinary diversity of human personalities you encounter. There is always one player who has been waiting their entire life for this particular match and will personally investigate every mistake you have made since the moment you installed Steam. Miss one last hit? Reported. Die to a gank? Reported. Buy the wrong item? Reported. Exist in the same geographical region as Russia? Probably reported. And yet, somehow, the same people who are threatening to uninstall the game, abandon the match, and report the entire team will still be playing another game approximately fourteen seconds after the Ancient explodes. Then there are the specialists. The carry who has spent 38 minutes farming and suddenly announces that the team needs to "play around me." The support who has purchased approximately 14 wards but has placed all of them in locations where absolutely nothing has ever happened. The mid player who dies twice and immediately begins constructing a legal case against the position 4. The offlaner who has been missing since minute six. And the mysterious player who says "trust me" immediately before doing something that results in four deaths. Somehow, despite all of this, you continue playing. Because every once in a while, Dota produces a moment so perfectly coordinated that you briefly understand why millions of people willingly subject themselves to this game. A smoke. A perfect initiation. Five enemy heroes caught. Spells flying everywhere. Your entire team screaming in celebration. The enemy Ancient falls. For a brief and beautiful moment, everyone loves each other. Then you queue again. And this is where Dota becomes truly impressive. It doesn't matter how many times you swear that this is your last game. Dota has perfected the psychological art of making you believe that the next match will be different. It won't. The next match will contain another Russian who is somehow both your teammate and your sworn enemy. Another person will type "gg" at minute eight. Someone will disconnect. Someone will buy an item that makes no sense. Someone will blame you for something that happened on the opposite side of the map. And you will sit there at 2:17 in the morning thinking: "Surely we can win the next one." Dota 2 is not a game you finish. It is a cycle you enter. You lose. You blame your team. Your team blames you. You promise never to play again. You queue again. You win. You experience an indescribable feeling of superiority. You queue again. You lose. And somewhere in the distance, a Russian player is typing something in all chat that is probably not appropriate for this review. 10/10. Terrible game. See you tomorrow.

**⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 10/10 — I hate this game** Dota 2 is not a game. It is a psychological experiment conducted on people who willingly click **“Find Match”** despite knowing exactly what is going to happen. And somehow… I love it. The gameplay is incredible. There is always something new to learn. Every hero can feel completely different, every match can turn into a 60-minute movie, and sometimes you pull off a play so beautiful that you briefly believe you are the greatest Dota player alive. Then your support walks into five enemies alone. Dies. Buys back. Does it again. Types **“team?”** Peak Dota. The best part is that you can spend 45 minutes carefully farming, warding, smoking, controlling Roshan and executing the perfect teamfight… …only for a guy named **xX_Destroyer420_Xx** to buy a Divine Rapier and run directly into the enemy fountain. **-25 MMR.** Beautiful. 10/10. I love the complexity, the strategy, the ridiculous heroes and the fact that literally anything can happen. I hate the matchmaking, griefers, smurfs, disconnects and that mysterious teammate who suddenly becomes a professional philosopher after dying once: **“gg.”** Overall: **80% amazing game. 20% emotional damage. 100% addiction.** Would recommend. Would I recommend playing ranked at 2 AM? Absolutely not. Will I do it tonight? **Yes.** Now please upvote this review. I need at least one victory today.

You can have an amazing game and accomplish something genuinely impressive, yet the game’s arbitrary systems can make it feel like none of it mattered. Get a rampage with Techies, for example, and somehow the progression system can barely acknowledge what you just did. The whole thing often feels less like measuring performance and more like rolling dice with a UI attached. And then comes the final masterpiece of incompetence: the endless updates. Valve seems to have developed the pathological need to change something simply because they feel they have to change something. Mechanics that were perfectly fine get needlessly redesigned, unnecessary systems are introduced, then later “fixed” when they inevitably make things worse. It is an endless cycle of changing things for the sake of changing them and then pretending the subsequent cleanup is meaningful development. Dota 2 is an incredible example of how a technically sophisticated game can become an absolutely exhausting experience through its own design philosophy. It feels like a game that has been deliberately optimized to keep you addicted, frustrated, competitive, and angry — and then offers you another match before you have time to ask yourself why you are still playing. At some point, you have to admire the achievement: they managed to turn a game into a punishment loop and convince millions of people to volunteer for it.

TL;DR Fantastic gameplay, heroes, and strategy. Awful punishment system and lack of meaningful support can make technical issues feel just as punishable as intentional abandoning. I enjoy the heroes, the strategy, and the cosmetic system, but the experience is often overshadowed by systems that feel unforgiving toward newer players. I even managed to reconnect, defended our Ancient during the final push, and we ended up winning. Despite returning and contributing to the victory, I was still forced to win five Single Draft matches as a penalty. The system doesn't seem to distinguish between players who intentionally abandon games and those who disconnect because of technical issues. As a result, the punishment feels unfair, especially when you've done everything you can to reconnect and help your team. I wish the game would let me get back to playing normally, or at least continue progressing through time-limited events. Instead of welcoming players back after an unfortunate disconnect, the punishment system pushes them away. It feels like players with genuine technical issues are treated the same as those who intentionally abandon matches or repeatedly engage in toxic behaviour. There doesn't seem to be any meaningful way to appeal these situations or have them reviewed, which only makes the experience more frustrating.

I don't play carry anymore. I play support now, and I have discovered the true meaning of Dota: I feed the enemy carry all game long. And you know what? He's having a GREAT time. Best game of his life. Rampage at minute 20. Somewhere out there, a 14-year-old is smiling because of me. Dota 2 is hands down the best MOBA on the market and for a while I shared the sentiment that it was the best game ever made. Gabe Newell plays it everyday and I think that it also is the best Valve game they have made. It got me interested in other MOBAs and liking the genre as a whole but in terms of execution, character viability, and existence of comeback mechanics, it by far makes this one the most rewarding to sink time into to get better. The game constantly evolves and while many people argue that it is more complicated now, in actuality the game is easier than when it released in 2012. I started playing in 2013 followed by a 4 year hiatus some time in between, picked up the game again and focusing on ranking up for the first time. Addressing the fact that the game is hard to understand is a natural part of the game. I have coached a few friends over the past 5 years and explained that it is okay for the game to not make sense. Similarly to playing chess it would be acceptable to not know what the pieces do and until you figure it out can you start to engage with the game and make sense of what to do and how to do it. You do not need to have a PHD to be able to play this game or find some enjoyment. I have found many people that can barely tie their own shoes and they manage just fine. Toxicity is not unique to this game but it does give you tools to be creative with it. Think of counter strike where the presence of toxicity is one thing but then you can blind with a flashbang, team kill, and so on and so forth. I still think hands down Dead By daylight is the most toxic game by far if I were to be completely honest based on my experience. The character design has the same flare that other valve games are known for so if the game is too competitive then there are player made games similar to what you'd find in Roblox or Garry's mod in the games "Arcade" which was one of the ways I eased a friends into playing the base game. The cosmetics are divided into components so you can mix and match allowing this feature to make the game into a dress up sim. In conclusion I do think everyone could find some degree of enjoyment in this type of game so long as there is an interest in wanting to both learn and improve.

The identity that made this game legendary has been stripped away in favor of chasing trends and selling cosmetics. New skins are uninspired garbage, while many of the classic ones that players actually loved have been removed. Every new "feature" or "mechanic" seems designed to bloat the game rather than improve it. System requirements keep climbing for no good reason, yet performance somehow keeps getting worse. Even on a modern PC, the game stutters, lags, and the servers frequently fail to respond. It's honestly embarrassing for a game that's been around this long. After thousands of hours invested, I've finally had enough. I'm going back to Dota 1—the original game that actually respected its own identity. Dota 2 stopped being a true successor years ago. Очень прикольная карта с идеальной расстановкой крипов,рун,лотусов,башен и много чего еще. Много различных режимов игры по типу All Pick, Turbo, Single draft и так далее. Красивые и интересные скины на практически все что есть в игре Ивенты. Например в данный момент есть ивент Dark Carnaval в котором играя вы можете получить много чего интересного, например, билеты которые в будущем вы сможете обменять на продвижение в поезде получая различные прикольные награды, также есть отедльная вкладка с камнем пророчества в которой вы можете гадать на картах таро не выходя даже из игры, что как по мне очень удобно и классно. Также очень круто реализованы способности, тобиж спеллы персонажей, например у моего любимого героя "Shadow Fiend" есть спелл, который называется "Shadowraze" в виде трех штук разной дальности, что помогает убивать множество противников и придумывать различные прокасты и тактики, еще у "Shadow Fiend" имеется очень крутая способность называемая "Feast of souls" которая делает его атаки невероятно быстрыми, и очень круто что у него еще есть пассивная способность под названием "Presence of the Dark Lord" которая снижает броню противникам в зоне действия, и конечно же есть очень классный ультимейт "Requiem of Souls" во время действия которого он выпускает накопленные души что накладывает на врагов эффект "Страх" из за которого враги начинают убегать от СФ'а что может помочь легче попасть койлами (shadowraze'ом) по врагам и в последствии убить их. Минусы: Единственный минус который я могу отметить так это то, что в режиме Turbo очень часто попадаются сильные игроки из за чего тяжело выигрывать катки, было бы очень круто если бы пересмотрели подбор врагов и сделали так чтобы кидало правда по уровню. В общем я думаю что игра очень даже хорошая и я советую ее вам потому что в ней много всякого благодаря чему на изучение игры уйдет не мало времени и у вас будет интерес в нее играть.

I've played League for 12+ years. I really like Dota 2 a lot. The micro seems less difficult than in League, but the cheese feels more extreme. I find myself focusing much more on macro play in Dota. In League, it's more about every tiny step—dodging skillshots, landing your own, and winning extended fights through constant maneuvering and looking for small windows of opportunity. With Dota, it feels more based around powerful point-and-click abilities and very over-the-top, often unavoidable hero powers. The game is often about setting up numerical advantages and catching people off guard with smoke. Both are fun in their own ways. I love all the active items in Dota and their relatively short cooldowns. It's a very fun game. I also really like how massive the jungle is—even as a support in very drawn-out games, I can end up with 300+ CS. I'd highly recommend this game to people coming from League. It might just refresh your love for MOBAs.

There’s a certain sentiment that games like League or Dota are an addiction, something that players can’t unlatch themselves from; the uninstall button evading every impulse, as the blood and sanity is sapped year after year. Endless reviews of people thousands of hours into the void, telling, warning people of its pull. I can’t agree with them. This game is even richer and more rewarding than when I started 11 years ago. While life drains every joy around me, Dota is the constant that provides endless engagement. The game is ever-changing. I can’t think of any other online experience that switches up the meta so frequently, and yet it rarely ever feels unbalanced or broken. This malleable game space is the reason nobody is clamouring for a Dota 3 — we’ve passed that point 8 mega-patches ago. Production value is consistent with Valve’s other games: polished to an unbelievable degree; impeccable sound design, you can close your eyes and still know what’s going on; slick Source 2 visuals; intuitive gameplay, options for options, play how you want. I think it helps a lot if you treat it entirely as a sport; framing something like this as a game implies victory at the end of the tunnel — credits, achievements, fulfilment. Not so. The only end is artificial, a truncation on the user’s end, be it shifting priorities, loss of interest, or death. You will lose. A lot. People that don’t realise this are only satisfied with those precious victories; maybe winning half the time is why so much resentment is visible online. Once you do reframe it, you’re free. Free to make friends as I have. Free to try new builds, new mind games, new team comps. Drag people through your off-lane Pugna arc. Bait enemies with your team, pull off the sickest 4 man black hole, get it cancelled by a rogue stun not meant for you. Blink into the enemy-infested fog and hook your reluctant teammate in. Engage with its complexities; this isn’t the sport for champions. Prepare to not just die, but lose. Every low met with a high, every report met with a commend, or a memory, or a friend, or just the buzz you need when everything around you persists at knocking you down. Lock in. Pump those hours, every one a notch of perseverance. Wave after wave, blood and adrenaline rising. Ten people in a gauntlet for courage, boldness and survival, each doing the only thing they can: their best. This is the sport for heroes.

☆☆☆☆☆ 0/5 A horrible MOBA with terrible matchmaking After more than 100 hours, I can confidently say that Dota 2 is a horrible MOBA overall and cannot come close to competing with League of Legends. Smurfing is one of the biggest problems. It feels like Valve does not care at all. Experienced players can buy cheap low-ranked accounts, stomp beginners and completely ruin matches. The pausing system is also ridiculous. People pause constantly, sometimes several times per game, and everyone else is forced to wait. Communication is often terrible too. Many players only speak Russian and refuse to use English, even when nobody else understands them. Some items are simply badly designed. Blink Dagger is a perfect example. When you are behind, enemies can camp in the jungle, blink onto you from outside your vision and instantly kill you. It feels like nowhere on the map is safe once your team starts losing. Other problems include: Clunky and delayed movement Extremely slow and overly long matches Confusing and overdesigned items Overloaded hero designs Weak and unsatisfying animations Bad matchmaking for beginners No proper party finder Worse laning than League Supports fighting carries for farm Uninteresting map objectives Smurfs, pauses and poor communication ruining games People often say Dota 2 is harder or deeper than League. Maybe it is more complicated, but complicated does not automatically mean better. Much of the gameplay feels based on cheesy tactics, invisibility, long stun chains and knowledge checks instead of satisfying mechanical outplays. League has plenty of problems, but its movement, pacing, laning, clarity and overall gameplay feel far superior. I gave Dota 2 more than enough chances. The more I played, the worse my opinion became. I cannot recommend it.

Pulling off a perfectly coordinated teamfight or executing a clutch play after careful planning gives an unmatched sense of satisfaction. The game rewards smart decision‑making, map awareness, and adaptability — not just mechanical skill. I also love how the developers keep the game fresh with regular updates, balance changes, and seasonal events. The battle passes and cosmetics are a nice touch, but they never feel pay‑to‑win; the focus stays on the gameplay. Plus, the built‑in tools for watching replays and studying pro matches are fantastic for improving your skills. The community can be intense (okay, sometimes downright toxic), but when you find good teammates, the cooperation and communication make the victories even sweeter. And for those who prefer a more relaxed experience, there’s a ton of custom content and fun game modes to enjoy. Graphically, the game still looks great, and the sound design and voice lines add so much character to each hero. Dota 2 isn’t just a game — it’s a whole ecosystem with tournaments, lore, and a passionate global community. If you’re into strategy, teamwork, and games that really test your mind, Dota 2 is an absolute must‑play. I’d give it 5/5.

Dota 2 is a moderately enjoyable game with a lot of depth, but it's far from being balanced. Some heroes feel noticeably stronger than others, which can make matches frustrating depending on the current meta. However, the biggest problem isn't the gameplay—it's the behavior score and reporting system. Players can report you for little to no reason, and those reports can significantly lower your behavior score, even if you didn't do anything wrong. Once your behavior score drops, you're forced into matches with toxic players, griefers, and ruiners who intentionally sabotage games. This creates a vicious cycle that's incredibly difficult to escape and makes the overall experience miserable. A competitive game should reward skill and teamwork, not punish players because of an unreliable reporting system. Unfortunately, this issue overshadows many of the game's strengths. Because of these problems, I can't recommend Dota 2 to anyone. While the core gameplay has potential, the player experience is too heavily affected by an unfair reporting system and the toxic environment it creates.

If you can use a keyboard and a mouse, if you can read, if you enjoy learning new mechanics, memorizing hundreds of abilities, item interactions, timings, counters, power spikes, map objectives, ward spots, smoke timings, rune control, stacking camps, pulling lanes, and approximately seventeen different ways a single hero can ruin your entire week... Congratulations. You are now qualified to complete the tutorial. Welcome to Dota 2. A game so beautifully designed that after 1,000 hours you'll still confidently say, "I have absolutely no idea what just happened in that fight." Other games teach you how to play. Dota teaches you humility. Every match is a fresh educational experience where you discover exciting new concepts such as: * Your hero is apparently useless against their hero. * Your items were wrong. * Your skill build was wrong. * Your positioning was wrong. * Existing was wrong. The learning curve isn't a curve. It's a vertical cliff covered in ice, and at the top stands a 12,000 hour veteran laughing while playing a hero you've never seen before. The ranking system is especially motivating. Play your heart out for three months to gain 300 MMR. Lose it all in one weekend because your carry decided farming jungle creeps during the final base defense was "the optimal macro play." Reach Herald? Congratulations. Reach Guardian? Impressive. Reach Crusader? Nice. Reach Ancient? Great. Reach Immortal? Wonderful. You'll still open the match and immediately be informed by your teammates that you are the worst player they have ever witnessed in human history. The community ensures you never develop dangerous levels of self-confidence. And the complexity... Oh, the complexity. There are heroes with more text in their abilities than some university textbooks. There are item interactions that require a law degree to understand. There are mechanics discovered by players ten years after release because apparently everyone collectively forgot they existed. Every patch note feels less like game balance and more like reading amendments to a country's constitution. Would I recommend Dota 2? Absolutely. If your dream is to suffer for eternity, question every life decision that led you here, develop Stockholm Syndrome with a video game, and after thousands of hours still be permanently trapped in the lower ranks wondering where it all went wrong... Then Dota 2 is the perfect game for you. 10/10.

Dota 2 es uno de los títulos más importantes y completos que ha dado el género MOBA. Su legado se remonta a los orígenes de Dota en Warcraft III: The Frozen Throne, una historia que no solo le otorga identidad propia, sino que también lo convierte en una de las comunidades más longevas y apasionadas de los videojuegos. A lo largo de los años, el juego ha evolucionado constantemente sin perder la esencia que lo hizo tan especial desde sus inicios. Uno de sus mayores atractivos es la enorme variedad de héroes, estrategias y estilos de juego. Cada partida puede desarrollarse de manera completamente distinta, ofreciendo una profundidad mecánica y táctica que pocos juegos logran alcanzar. La curva de aprendizaje puede ser exigente, pero precisamente esa complejidad es la que hace que cada mejora personal se sienta realmente significativa. El sistema de progresión también merece reconocimiento. Dota 2 ofrece una gran cantidad de elementos cosméticos, arcanas, personas, avatares, locutores y otros elementos visuales que pueden obtenerse tanto mediante tiempo de juego como a través de compras. Lo importante es que estos elementos no afectan el rendimiento dentro de las partidas: la habilidad del jugador sigue siendo el factor más determinante. El progreso competitivo depende del conocimiento, la práctica y la experiencia, no del dinero invertido. Más allá de sus sistemas y mecánicas, Dota 2 tiene una capacidad muy particular para crear recuerdos. Para muchos jugadores, las partidas compartidas con amigos terminan convirtiéndose en una parte importante de sus vidas. En mi caso, algunos de mis mejores recuerdos nacieron jugando con amigos del colegio, desde que teníamos alrededor de 13 años hasta hoy, superando ya los 30. Son años de victorias, derrotas, madrugadas, torneos y conversaciones que van mucho más allá del propio juego. No obstante, Dota 2 también presenta aspectos negativos que no pueden ignorarse. Su comunidad puede ser extremadamente tóxica, especialmente en las partidas clasificatorias. El sistema de MMR, que mide el nivel competitivo del jugador, puede resultar frustrante cuando se juega en solitario, ya que el progreso muchas veces depende del desempeño de cuatro compañeros adicionales. Esto hace que subir de rango pueda convertirse en una experiencia agotadora y desmotivante para muchos jugadores. En contraste, jugar en grupo transforma completamente la experiencia. Compartir estrategias, coordinar jugadas y disfrutar las partidas con amigos convierte incluso las derrotas en momentos memorables. Dota 2 alcanza su mejor versión cuando se vive como una experiencia colectiva. Actualmente ya no lo juego de manera activa, pero puedo afirmar que Dota 2 fue mucho más que un videojuego. Para muchas personas representa una etapa de la vida, una forma de mantener amistades y una colección de recuerdos que permanecen incluso años después de dejar de jugar. Pocos títulos pueden presumir de generar ese nivel de conexión emocional con sus jugadores.

Thank You for Making Me Quit — A Dota 2 Review After 10+ Years Hours played: more than a decade Recommendation: It's complicated. Thank you, Valve. Thank you for finally making me quit Dota 2. I mean that with all the bitterness it deserves, because for me this was never just a game. For over ten years, Dota was where my friends and I showed up for each other. It was there through the depression, the heartbreaks, the family problems, and the goodbyes when friends left the country to work abroad. When life was falling apart, the queue was still there. We'd load in, pick our heroes, talk trash, lose, win, and somehow feel a little less alone. That was the real game. The matches were just the excuse to keep coming back to each other. We don't play every day — life doesn't allow that anymore. But when we do get to sit down and queue together, we play it serious. We value teamwork above everything else. That's the whole point for us: five people moving as one, trusting each other to do their part. We played ranked — not to flex, but because ranked was supposed to mean something. It was supposed to be the mode where everyone tried, where you weren't dropped into a lobby with someone treating a serious match like their first day on the game. We queued up as a duo, as a trio, sometimes a full stack of five, and for years that was enough. But these last months — these last couple of years — every update seems to break something. The matchmaking feels broken in a way it never used to. Smurfs everywhere. Teammates who clearly have no idea what their role is supposed to do. You queue solo, or as two, or as three, and there's almost always that one random filling out the team who doesn't have a clue — and that's all it takes to turn a match into a stress test instead of a game. That's the part that hurts. Ranked was supposed to fix exactly this. It was supposed to balance the lobby so everyone could actually compete and have fun. Instead it's become the thing causing the stress. The thing draining the fun out of the one place my friends and I went to escape the stress. Maybe that's the real review here: the game changed. Not the graphics, not the heroes — the feeling. The thing that kept us coming back for ten years quietly stopped being there. I'm not angry at Dota. I'm grateful for what it gave us. I'm just tired of fighting the matchmaking to get back something that used to come easy. So thank you, Dota — for the decade, the memories, and the friendships that outlasted every patch. And thank you, finally, for making it easy to walk away.

Dota 2 is a free to play MOBA that originally started it's life as a mod in Warcraft 3. I want to start off this review by saying that this game is very complex, while you can learn the basics of the game in a few matches the underlying mechanics will take you many hundred to understand. If your looking for something to pick up and play this probably isn't it unless your willing to learn over a hundred hours or more. The game is free to play but unlike other free to play games all purchases in Dota are purely cosmetic and add no advantage or pay to win mechanics, as more games should be. For those unfamiliar a MOBA consists a 5v5 game on a 3 lane map. 2 heroes go top and bottom and 1 usually will go middle. There a certain heroes who excel in certain roles that you will eventually learn over time. In recent years Dota has added a new player learning section which is great for people new to MOBAs or Dota in general. It covers not just a MOBA but also mechanics specific to Dota I will take about later. A typical match in Dota will last between 30 and 75 minutes but have lasted all the way up to close to over 3 hours in a pro level match before. There are so many different mechanics that have an impact on a match that no 2 matches will ever feel the same. For the majority of my review I will be comparing Dota 2 to it's main competitor League of Legends and then I will get into other details on Dota after. For starters Dota 2 has far less heroes than League of Legends at 127 currently compared to 171 in League of Legends. Despite needing to learn more heroes League of Legends is actually an easier MOBA to play, however because of that fact it's also boring and games are pretty predictable. If you lose the laning phase it's very hard to come back in League of Legends because there are no game changing items you can buy. In Dota 2 there are items such as Black King Bar (BKB) which makes you 100% immune to magic damage, which is 1 of the 3 types of damage from hero abilities in Dota. There are other items to like the blink dagger which allows you to teleport a certain distance around you to gank enemies. There are many different items in Dota that can allow you to come back from a few deaths at the start of the game. You also don't lose gold when you die in league making getting items a little easier where as in Dota you lose a % of gold and the other team gets gold each kill. In League of Legends the laning phase also changes to 2 bottom 1 top 1 mid and 1 jungle right away which is roaming the map and killing the mobs for gold and xp. In Dota even the high damage carry heroes need a few levels before being able to farm the jungle. In League of Legends you also don't have camp stacking. In Dota when farming jungle or in the early game the support heroes and sometimes mid will go around and pull jungle mobs from there spawn. If they are out of the spawn box at the start of each new minute a new stack will spawn and if you run away from the pulled mobs they will return effectively leaving 2 groups on the jungle camp. The person who makes the stacked camp gets XP and Gold once those are killed even if not by themselves. This is just another big mechanic in Dota that allows you to come back or get ahead of the other team. Dota has much more mechanics to watch for in the laning phase as well such as "Denying" or killing your own creeps before the other team does. This will give the other team half the XP they normally would and denies them getting gold from the last hit. Both games feature the same last hit mechanics requiring you to be the final person to hit a creep to their death to get any gold. However in league there is no turn rate so u don't need to face the creep to hit it where as in Dota each hero has its own timing to turn and face the creep and it's own timing to hit the creep you will need to account for. Again this is just another way to get an advantage back to your team if you die in the laning phase, just getting more last hits and denying the other teams gold and XP will help. Lastly Dota 2 is harder because you can't see over stairs. The game uses a 3D model where league you can basically see anywhere expect hiding in a bush or something. Enemies can be waiting at the top of the stairs and you wouldn't know without climbing up or placing wards to see. This makes movement very different in Dota and can lead to some bad deaths and emphasizes the importance of placing wards for vision. Dota also applies a 25% chance to miss your target such as a creep if they are above you, this is most common for the midlaner who fights between 2 stairs. While these mechanics make the game far more challenging to play and learn, they do create many options for a game to turn out and for that I rate it a 10/10 for game mechanics. The game gets a new update about once a month constantly balancing heroes and changing the content and mechanics in the game. This is frustrating to learn all the time but also keeps the game ever changing and well balanced as it's hard to make 127 heroes feel perfectly balanced. It also shows the devs care a lot about the game. Dota 2 has had a huge esports scene in the past but for some reason they decided to make a couple large tournaments throughout the year rather than host The International (TI) as a big event. Personally I think this is a 1/10. As someone who didn't play much Dota in the past the big TI prize pools caught my eye and brought in new players like myself to see what this game is all about. I think if Valve wants to make different tournaments have decent prize pools go back to the old model of community funded battle passes and cosmetics to go back to the prize pool and just host multiple passes throughout the year for different tournaments. The tournaments are still large but it does attract media away from Dota and towards other titles with higher payouts as well as gamers and teams trying to make a profitable living. Look how many people were playing Fortnite and head of the game over their 100M dollar tournament years ago. Steam should be advertising the tournament on their store page when it was 20-40M for the TI. It's a big deal and the qualifier rounds and main tournament coverage should be posted to attract new viewers and players. Overall Dota is a great game, it falls in line with Valves other games like Counter Strike in the fact that it is easy to run. Valve also has 2 giants in the market making them a ton of revenue on top of steam sales commissions that this game isn't going anywhere anytime soon. I would recommend playing this game and trying to learn it for 100 hours which will allow you to finally play the ranked mode and get matched with people around the same skill as you. used to enjoy Dota 2, but the ranked system has become one of the most frustrating parts of the game. The MMR system feels like it only punishes players instead of rewarding improvement. You can play well, carry your team, and still lose because of one bad teammate. A single game can ruin hours of progress. The Behavior Score and Communication Score system also feels unfair and unclear. You can try to play normally, but one bad match, a few reports, or arguments with teammates can lower your score and put you with even worse players. It feels like the system does not always understand the difference between a toxic player and someone just having a bad game. The community is one of the biggest problems. Too many games are ruined by people flaming, blaming teammates, giving up early, or intentionally ruining the match. A good team game becomes stressful because you spend more time dealing with players than actually enjoying the game. Dota 2 has amazing heroes, deep strategy, and great gameplay, but the matchmaking and player behavior systems need a lot of improvement. New players especially will have a hard time staying interested when every match feels like a punishment. Great game idea, but the ranked experience and community make it hard to enjoy.

But for some reason, it feels like you've deliberately decided to kill it. First, why was All Random removed from the game? Was it bothering anyone? Why are you removing features that were already implemented and enjoyed by players? Second, as a regular player who doesn't want to play ranked because every other match is filled with boosters who are clearly above my skill level, I mostly play Turbo. So why am I still being matched against players who are significantly better than me? When are you finally going to create proper skill-based matchmaking? Why am I so often placed against players who are on a completely different level? Third, your so-called "50% system" is one of the worst ideas imaginable. The most enjoyable matches in Dota are games where both teams are evenly matched in skill. Because of this system, those games only happen about one out of ten times. Instead, your matchmaking seems to put one or several weak players on the enemy team so that I can win. But that's not fun. Winning because the other team has inexperienced players isn't satisfying. On the other hand, when the weak player ends up on my team and we're facing much stronger opponents, that's equally terrible. Nobody enjoys getting stomped because the teams are unbalanced. As a result, this "50% system" is one of the worst possible solutions to the matchmaking problem. Players don't want forced win rates - they want fair and balanced games. Fourth, why did you ruin The International prize pools? Every year The International feels less exciting and less important than it used to. Why not bring back the system that allowed players to contribute to and increase the prize pool? That was one of the things that made TI special and helped create the biggest event in esports. Fifth, why are balance changes being handled by people who, judging by the results, seem to have little understanding of the game? Many recent patches feel disconnected from what players actually want. Bring back the people who were working on the game 10 years ago! I've been playing Dota 2 for so long that at this point I'm not entirely sure whether I play Dota or Dota plays me. The weird thing is I don't even grind ranked anymore. Turbo is where it's at. My friends and I treat Dota 2 like that old reliable restaurant you've been going to for years. You know the menu. You know exactly what you're getting. You know you'll probably complain about it while you're there. And yet somehow you keep coming back. Every time a new game comes out, the group gets excited. "We're definitely playing this for months." Two weeks later the Discord call goes quiet. Somebody eventually says the magic words: "Dota?" And just like that, ten years of gaming innovation gets thrown into a ditch. Back to Turbo. Back to chaos. Back to five grown adults making terrible decisions at maximum speed. That's what makes Turbo so good. Nobody cares. People are picking heroes they haven't touched in three years. Someone is building items that should probably violate international law. Your friend swears his build is "secret tech" even though it's currently 4-12 and being investigated by multiple human rights organizations. And somehow it still works. Sometimes. The matches are fast enough that losing doesn't feel like you've wasted an evening. You get stomped? Whatever. Queue again. Twenty minutes later you're all laughing because a fully farmed support just deleted somebody from existence using what appears to be a kitchen utensil and raw confidence. The best part isn't even the game anymore. It's the people. Dota has become less of a game and more of a digital pub where the activity is yelling at each other while occasionally remembering to destroy the Ancient. Half the fun is listening to your friends confidently announce a terrible plan and then watching it unfold exactly as badly as expected. The game itself is somehow still amazing after all these years. Every match creates a different kind of stupidity. Some games feel like a tactical war. Others feel like five shopping carts crashing into each other in a supermarket parking lot. Both are equally entertaining. Sure, Dota has problems. The learning curve is less of a curve and more of a vertical cliff covered in broken glass. The community can occasionally make you question the future of humanity. And every patch somehow manages to make heroes stronger, weaker, stronger again, then somehow turn a support into a raid boss. But none of that really matters. Because when the group has nothing new to play, Dota is always there. Waiting. Patiently. Like an old friend. Or a highly intelligent curse. Right. Time to queue Turbo and immediately regret trusting my teammates with anything more complicated than breathing.

Its a game with a dangerous combination, its quite addicting but fundamentally broken at a root level, perhaps by design. The game itself at its core is fun, the heroes are fun to play, and the game is updated semi-often (although the quality and quantity of said updates has significantly declined in the last few years). Theirs no game quite like Dota 2, theirs over 100 heroes, all of them play completely differently, with their own skills and item builds, no two heroes feel the same. When playing with a stack theirs quite alot of thought that goes into your draft, your item build and your skill build. When it clicks its very addictive and quite honestly very fun. Nothing gives you a better dopamine hit than getting a rampage. Or winning that really close 50 minute game. But good lord the games horribly designed, to begin with, this game is unbelievably complicated, staring at the screen, youll see numbers and graphics everywhere, even basic skills and abilities can have half a page of text explaining what they do, items can too. This isnt a casual game that you play for a little while and move on, this is a game you play for life, or you dont play it at all. Even before you pick a hero to play, the fundamental basics of the game take months to learn, your looking at years of investment before your anywhere close to "good", thats just how complicated and in-depth this game is. If you want to play a new hero for example, youll need to read guides, watch videos and replays. You might be ok on a hero initially, but without going off and doing a bunch of research, you'll just end up throwing games and having people rage at you, this isnt a game, its a second job, in most cases it feels like your primary job. Then theirs the large patches that come out every 2-3 months, Dota 2 patches can be quite big. Dozens of pages and notes affecting huge amounts of heroes, items and even the map. Every time a release comes out you may have your favourite item or hero completely reworked entirely, meaning you effectively have to learn them again every 6-12 months, depending on the hero. Even worse, some patches completely change the basics of the game so drastically it feels like your playing a whole new game, this happens often. But perhaps the biggest design flaw of this game is the way it handles advantages in the early and mid game. When you get kills, you get money and experience, same with towers. Money lets you buy items to get stronger, experience helps you level up so you can get more stats and abilities. If one team gets an early lead, assuming a somewhat equal draft, then coming back is almost impossible since just being ahead gives you an advantage so you can get even more ahead, Dota 2 is an EXTREMELY snowball heavy game, once the snowball starts rolling, stopping it becomes almost impossible. The old saying "whoever gets ahead stays ahead" should be the motto of this game. In the rare case you do manage to pull off a comeback, its because the enemy team has made a series of major mistakes to let your team back in, rarely is it because you “outplayed” anyone. This snowball methodology becomes so laughable that even if you do outplay the other team, you often wont get a kill just because the enemy team is so tanky, and your own items are so far behind that kills becomes significantly more difficult. The game actively prohibits better teams winning if they lose the mid/eary game because they are just too far behind to catchup. Cores with a gold/experience lead can legitimately wipe 3-4 enemy heroes on their own. Think of it this way, your playing tennis and you get a break of serve, your now ahead, as a result of you getting that break of serve, your own serve is now 25% faster, you move 25% quicker and your 25% less tired. This is the basic premise in Dota 2, you get a significant advantage just for being ahead, this happens in no other sport, you dont get to move 25% faster just because you sunk a three pointer in basketball. You dont get to throw a pitch 25% faster because you just struck someone out previously in a game of baseball. How many games of NBA have you watched where the teams that ends up winning, has a slow start? Or has a bad first quarter only to come back and win? In Dota 2, if you have a bad start and your around 10k gold behind, your chances of winning are just 25%. You cant just "change tactics", the game fundementaly and statistically tries its best to prevent come backs by giving people huge statistical advantages JUST FOR BEING AHEAD. This even makes WATCHING games boring, because as soon as you see that 10k number come up you may as well do something else. Moreover, stomps are VERY common in this game. 4/5 games are stomps where you know whose going to win after the first 10 or so minutes, where Dota 2 shines is that 1/5 game that goes down to the wire and you win. The addiction comes when you try to chase that same feeling and game for the next 3 days in vain. The other critical flaw in this game is just how minimal you can feel in terms of impact. You are 1 of 10 players, so even though you may be playing a great game, it doesnt matter if two other people on your team are just playing for laughs and giggles and end up dying alot in the early part of the game. Conversely, youll often win games where you play terribly, because someone else in your team is stomping everyone else. The only role that is absolutely critical is the position 1 role, you can win games with bad supports or an average mid, but you wont win with a terrible position 1. This often means that support players often feel like wins are out of their hands, it can be incredibly deflating when your playing fantastic as a support, but your position 1 feed 5 kills in the opening 2 minutes. The other aspect of this game that often gets overlooked is just how toxic games can be. This isnt COD or BF2 where games last 15 minutes, you can leave whenever you want and no one really talks because its just a goofy, fun game where no one really cares that much. Dota 2 games can last 50 minutes, thats a long time to be stuck with the same 4 people on your team, if things are going badly, people can get toxic very quickly, and you cant leave or quit before the game ends since theres no surrender button. If your behind as per my above point, comebacks just dont happen that often, and as a result its not uncommon to be sitting in a game that was over 15 minutes ago, just watching you and your team mates die over and over again for 20 minutes. This game brings out the worst in people, you absolutely have to have very thick skin to play this game, its not for the timid or shy. In the end, I have over 9000 hours in this game, most of the time I have not enjoyed, but due to how addicting it can be, stopping becomes challenging. If you do take the plunge and dedicate serious amounts of time and effort into this game, quitting becomes even harder because youve already dedicated a huge amount of time already, time you dont want to feel like youve "wasted". I often think about what I could have done with those 9000 hours, what skills I could have developed or interests I could have pursued. Dont be like me, I hate this game and I wish I never played it.

Won your lane? Doesn't matter. Your carry is currently farming the jungle while the enemy destroys your Ancient and typing, "gg team no support." The learning curve of Dota 2 isn't a curve. It's a vertical concrete wall coated in cooking oil. New players enter a match and immediately discover there are 100+ heroes, hundreds of abilities, dozens of items, countless mechanics, and approximately 4 million ways to embarrass themselves in front of strangers. The community is one of the greatest social experiments ever conducted. Nowhere else can you find five people with completely different backgrounds united by a shared belief that every loss is somebody else's fault. A typical Dota 2 match consists of: One guy who thinks he's the next world champion. One guy playing music through his microphone. One guy whose internet is powered by a hamster. One guy who hasn't spoken all game but suddenly writes a 500-word essay explaining why everyone else is terrible. And you, wondering why you didn't just watch a movie instead. The game is so addictive that players will spend 60 minutes suffering through the most miserable match imaginable, swear they'll never play again, close the game, stare at the desktop for 30 seconds, and immediately queue for another match. The heroes themselves are absurd. Some are gods, dragons, demons, and ancient cosmic entities capable of destroying worlds. Yet all of them can be beaten to death by a shirtless guy with an axe who runs at people screaming. The matchmaking system deserves its own award. Somehow it consistently creates games where both teams are convinced they received the worse players. Dota 2 isn't a game. It's a relationship. A toxic, emotionally damaging relationship that occasionally gives you one incredible victory just to keep you from leaving. And that's why millions of players keep coming back. Because deep down, every Dota player believes the next game will be different. It won't. Queue accepted. 🎮💀

Prieš žaisdamas „Dota 2“, vieninteliai vaizdo žaidimų personažai, su kuriais susidūriau, buvo „Starcraft“, „Warcraft“, „Command and Conquer“, „Battle Realms“, „Tekken“ (išskyrus „Kangą“), „Street Fighter“, įvairiuose japoniškuose RPG ir kt. Visuose šiuose žaidimuose moterys personažai visada buvo žmonių arba humanoidų pavidalo. Net ir nehumanoidės moterys visada galėjo transformuotis į humanoidus. Būsiu atvira, visos moteriškos personažai tuose žaidimuose man atrodė kaip merginos, net kai jos turėjo būti šiurpios (kaip Kerrigan dujų maišai su krūtinėmis ir chitininiai stiletai arba Banshees „Warcraft“), ​​jos vis tiek atrodė seksualios savaip groteskiškai (niekada nemačiau moteriškų personažų, kurie atrodytų kaip Bane, Night Stalker arba atrodytų kaip vyresni nei 30 metų tuo metu). Įsivaizduokite mano nuostabą, kai jie perkėlė Winter Wyvern į „Dota 2“ ir išgirdau, kad jos balsas buvo moteriškas. Pagalvojau: ką? Moterys negali būti drakonais? Tada supratau, kad vau, niekada anksčiau nemačiau moteriškos drakonės, kuri neturėtų žmogaus pavidalo. Drakonai visada buvo vyrai arba visada buvo pateikiami kaip vyrai žaidimuose, kuriuos žaidžiau (o jų žaidžiau daugybę), ir niekada nesupratau, kad moterys niekada nebuvo. Net kai jie perdarė Enchantress (jos kakta buvo padidinta) ir Broodmother (jos moteriškos akys buvo pašalintos ir paliktos tik įprastos voro akys) personažų modelius, buvau suglumęs, kaip jie man padarė juos „bjauresnius“. Tada supratau, palaukite, aš mačiau tiek daug monstriškų vyriškų personažų, bet niekada moterų. Kodėl taip yra? Tada supratau, kad tokie personažai kaip Medusa ir Spectre taip pat egzistuoja, ir aš niekada nemačiau tokių moteriškų personažų dizainų. Tokia išvaizda dažniausiai būdavo deleguojama blogiukams ar antraeiliams personažams, bet ne tikriems personažams, su kuriais žaisdavai. Šiaip ar taip, Dota 2 (prieš „Overwatch“) privertė mane suprasti, kad moterų archetipai žaidimuose yra labai riboti. Nesakau, kad negalime turėti merginų, bet keista, kad vaikystėje žaidžiau žaidimus ir niekada nesupratau, kad moterys gali būti daugiau nei tiesiog seksualios merginos. Manau, kad „Dota 2“ tikrai pralenkė savo laiką kurdama moteriškus personažus. Vienintelė priežastis, kodėl jie nesukūrė daugiau, buvo ta, kad dauguma moteriškų personažų „Dota 1“ (tie keli, kurie egzistavo) buvo perkelti iš „Warcraft 3“. Jei jie būtų pradėję nuo nulio, jie būtų galėję pasinerti į retesnius moterų archetipus. Dabar jie turi tokius personažus kaip Snapfire (sena moteris), Dark Willow, Hoodwink (patelė, kuri tiesiog atrodo kaip paprastas gyvūnas, o ne seksuali moteris su kailiu) ir Dawnbreaker (seksuali raumeninga moteris, kuri nedėvi drabužių spintos gedimo, laukiančio, kol įvyks).

You have become COMPLETELY dependent on your teammates. The International 2025 This led to The International 2025 becoming the longest tournament in the game's history. Dota 2 is not just a game — it’s a life experience you never agreed to. You enter saying “just one relaxed match,” and 10 minutes later someone is questioning your entire existence in three different languages. Every game starts with hope. Real hope. “This time I’ll win.” Then mid feeds, the carry is farming like it’s a single-player RPG, and your support disappears into the jungle saying “I carry.” At that point, the only thing truly coordinated is everyone’s suffering. The funny part is the end. No matter what happens — stomp, comeback, or total disaster — someone types “gg easy” like the last 45 minutes were a peaceful walk in the park instead of emotional damage simulation. And yet… you don’t uninstall. You tell yourself “one more game.” Then another. Then suddenly it’s 3 AM and you’re arguing with strangers about who ruined your life. Dota 2 doesn’t teach you how to win. It teaches you how to accept pain, blame your team, and still queue again tomorrow.

After several matches, I developed symptoms of hypertension, emotional damage, and possibly obesity from stress-eating during ranked games. This game did not just test my skills — it tested my blood pressure, my friendships, my morality, and my will to continue trusting strangers on the internet. The gameplay is incredibly deep and challenging. Every match feels different, mostly because you never know whether your teammate is a tactical genius, a future philosopher, or someone learning how a keyboard works for the first time. The strategy, hero combinations, and team fights are amazing, but the real challenge is surviving the chat. Dota 2 made me think twice about humanity. It made me question life. It made me wonder how five people can enter a game with the same goal and somehow become each other’s greatest enemies within 10 minutes. Still, despite the stress, the shouting, the questionable decisions, and the occasional urge to uninstall, Dota 2 remains one of the most exciting and rewarding games ever made. Winning a hard match feels like graduating, getting promoted, and receiving medical clearance all at the same time.

Well… what can I even say about Dota 2? I’ve played this game for over 9000 hours, and I’ll probably play for 9000 more. I’ve met some of the best people here, and also some of the absolute worst. Figuring out which is which adds its own little surprise mechanic outside the actual game xD Sometimes this game gets so addictive that I play for 30–40 hours straight, then suddenly realize I’m completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ up my life, uninstall it, and reinstall it again a week later because no other game comes close to challenging my brain, patience, coordination, and split-second decision making like this one does. Dota became more than just a game for me a long time ago. It’s like this weird personal fantasy world I escape into. Sometimes I come here when life is going badly, sometimes I come here to celebrate when life is going well. I’m also kind of an introvert IRL. I don’t fake socialize just for the sake of it, so sometimes when my friends are online, I’ll literally just sit in Discord, watch them play, and listen to the background conversations. Somehow that feels like socializing to me. I’ve played this game while happy, frustrated, depressed, angry, motivated — every possible emotional state. Sometimes I spread positive vibes all game, sometimes I wanna grief my teammates because I’m tilted at life itself. My teammates and enemies have definitely paid the price for whatever emotional state I was in that day lmao. Playing with a good group can be one of the most fun experiences ever… and also one of the most annoying. Sometimes your friends play like complete noobs, give unsolicited advice, or try to micromanage your hero like they’re playing the game for you. Honestly, playing Dota is basically like being in a marriage. Sometimes toxic. Sometimes amazing. Sometimes frustrating. Sometimes the best thing in your life. It’s this weird love/hate toxic/amazing relationship. Sometimes I feel like queueing solo anonymously so I can do whatever the ♥♥♥♥ I want with zero consequences. Other times I just wanna stack with a huge group, mess around, socialize, and have fun together. Then sometimes 5v5 lobbies become so tryhard that people start getting tilted and stop having fun entirely. Dota is basically life in game form. Very fun, very hard, sometimes toxic, sometimes beautiful, but always exciting. I honestly don’t know if I would recommend this game to anyone. But if someone asked me what the best game I’ve ever played is? Dota will probably always be at the top of the list. This game has seen every version of me, and I’ve seen every version of other people through it too. It’s hard to explain. Kinda like life itself lol.
